title: US Energy Chief Says Saudi Pipeline Should Reopen Within Days, Washington Sits on $50B for Nuclear Waste With No Repository, and Two Tankers Hit Mines Near Hormuz
subhead: US Energy Department officials said a key Saudi oil pipeline should be back online within days even as civil defense alerts briefly sounded in Dhahran, Dammam, and Abqaiq and two oil tankers struck mines near the Strait of Hormuz. In the United States, North Dakota regulators projected steady crude output and rising second-half oilfield activity as the domestic rig count ticked higher, while industry reports highlighted a $50 billion nuclear waste fund with no permanent repository and a domestic uranium fuel bottleneck.

sections.heading: Saudi Oil Pipeline Expected Back Within Days as Tankers Hit Mines Near Hormuz
sections.body:
The US Energy Secretary stated that a damaged Saudi Arabian oil pipeline is expected to return to service within days, offering potential relief to physical crude markets strained by eight months of Gulf conflict (EnergyNow). However, security risks around the kingdom's eastern energy corridor persisted on Saturday night as Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense Directorate briefly activated warning sirens in Dhahran — home to Saudi Aramco's headquarters — as well as Abqaiq, Dammam, and Al-Ahsa during clashes with Houthi forces before giving an all-clear (Times of Israel, Anadolu Agency).

In the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced that two oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire after turning off their navigation systems and attempting passage through an unauthorized route, while the United Arab Emirates rescued 22 sailors in nearby waters (Anadolu Agency, Al Jazeera). Separately, US Central Command fired on and disabled a commercial cargo ship attempting to breach the naval blockade in the Gulf of Oman and stood up a new task force to interdict Iranian overland supply routes (AP News, CBS News).

Crude prices traded flat to slightly lower heading into the weekend as traders weighed Iranian statements that dozens of authorized vessels were transiting Hormuz against International Energy Agency (IEA) surplus forecasts and the prospect of post-midterm ceasefire talks (EnergyNow).
sections.whyItMatters: Even if Saudi pipeline capacity is restored within days, mine strikes on tankers with disabled transponders and live gunfire in the Gulf of Oman keep war-risk insurance premiums elevated for every barrel leaving the Gulf.

sections.heading: US Holds $50B for Nuclear Waste With No Repository and Faces a Fuel Supply Wall
sections.body:
As Finland prepares to open the world's first permanent deep geological repository for spent nuclear fuel, the United States remains deadlocked with more than $50 billion collected for nuclear waste management and no permanent disposal facility to put it in, according to an analysis by OilPrice. Decades of political turnover and state-level opposition have left spent fuel stored at reactor sites across the country.

At the same time, America's broader nuclear power revival is running into a domestic uranium and nuclear fuel supply bottleneck (OilPrice). Although the United States operates the largest nuclear generation fleet in the world, it has added only one new nuclear power plant over the past decade, and domestic enrichment and conversion capacity remains insufficient to match surging power demand from artificial intelligence data centers (OilPrice).

Meanwhile, US clean-hydrogen ambitions have also slowed sharply, with several major regional hydrogen hubs stalling amid federal funding cuts and weaker-than-expected commercial off-take demand (OilPrice).
sections.whyItMatters: Tech companies and utilities are counting on nuclear power to supply round-the-clock electricity for AI data centers, but unresolved fuel enrichment bottlenecks and spent-fuel gridlock limit how fast new capacity can be built.

sections.heading: North Dakota Projects Steady Oil Output and Higher Second-Half Drilling as US Rig Count Rises
sections.body:
State energy regulators in North Dakota expect crude oil production in the Bakken shale play to remain steady despite recent price volatility, projecting that oilfield drilling and completion activity will rise in the second half of the year (EnergyNow). Supporting that outlook, the weekly US oil rig count ticked higher for the week ending November 7 (Anadolu Agency).

In the downstream and aviation sectors, however, high jet fuel costs and airspace disruptions continue to weigh on carriers. International Airlines Group (IAG), the parent company of British Airways, announced cuts to its capacity growth and capital investment plans citing elevated fuel expenses, while Maldives-focused luxury carrier BeOnd canceled all scheduled flights between October 30 and November 30 due to regional security conditions (Wall Street Journal, Dünya).
sections.whyItMatters: Steady US shale output provides a buffer against Gulf supply shocks, yet sustained high refine-product and jet fuel costs are already forcing major European airlines to trim capacity.

sections.heading: Egypt Approves Energy Rationing Plan Ahead of Antalya COP31 Summit
sections.body:
The Egyptian government approved an emergency fiscal and energy conservation package on Saturday aimed at insulating the economy from regional conflict fallout, mandating reductions in electricity and fuel consumption, cuts to public spending, and the deferral of select state investment projects (Anadolu Agency). The austerity measures accompany Cairo's parallel push to attract billions of dollars in foreign upstream investment to lift domestic natural gas output to 6.6 billion cubic feet per day by 2027 (OilPrice).

In neighboring Iraq, Environment Minister Sirwa Abdulwahid stated that the planned Development Road Project linking Gulf ports to Turkey will strengthen economic and energy transit ties across the region, while in Eastern Europe Russian overnight strikes damaged energy facilities in the Kyiv region (Anadolu Agency, Euronews).

Globally, energy analysts cited by OilPrice noted that the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East are accelerating electric vehicle adoption and gas demand destruction ahead of next week's COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, even as Wall Street 'energy transition' funds face scrutiny for holding heavy positions in natural gas producers (OilPrice, Milliyet).
sections.whyItMatters: Egypt's simultaneous move to ration domestic power while courting foreign gas drillers illustrates the squeeze facing energy-importing Middle Eastern states caught between wartime fuel prices and tight fiscal budgets.

bottomLine: Physical energy infrastructure in the Gulf remained on a knife-edge this weekend as US energy officials projected a damaged Saudi oil pipeline would restart within days, even while warning sirens sounded in Dhahran and Abqaiq and two tankers hit mines near Hormuz. In the United States, North Dakota regulators forecast steady Bakken crude output and rising US rig counts, but a pair of nuclear industry assessments warned that America's nuclear revival faces a domestic fuel bottleneck and $50 billion in unplaced nuclear waste. As delegates prepare for next week's COP31 summit in Antalya, Egypt enacted mandatory electricity and fuel conservation measures while British Airways parent IAG trimmed capacity over fuel costs.
sources: OilPrice, EnergyNow, Wall Street Journal, AP News, Al Jazeera, CBS News, Times of Israel, Euronews, IEA, Anadolu Agency, Dünya, Milliyet
